segments.t: Trouble strikes the space restaurant when the alien Emperor sends his dish back over a salt allergy, and Chef Barinov discovers that his own kitchen clone messed up the order.
Виктор Петрович, гость отказался от блюда.
Что не понравилось этому гостю?
У него сильная аллергия на соль.
Говорит, это не ресторан, а забегаловка.
Вы что там, совсем с ума сошли?
Император уже полжизни заказ ждёт!
Я перед ним анекдоты рассказываю.
Кто сегодня готовил это блюдо?
Слушай, через минуту блюдо будет готово.
Император недоволен, он нас уничтожит!
Кстати, а где мой клон?
Он должен был меня заменить.
А он вас уже заменил, шеф!
Let's walk through the climax of Chef Barinov's sci-fi daydream.
Виктор Петрович, гость отказался от блюда.
'Viktor Petrovich, the guest refused the dish.' Lyova establishes a brisk approach beside Barinov, combining "gost" ("guest") and "otkazalsya" ("refused") so the key meaning lands right away.
Что не понравилось этому гостю?
'What did this guest not like?' Barinov probes sharply in the room, pairing "ponravilos" ("pleased, was liked") with "gostyu" ("to the guest") so the "-sya" ending carries the action.
У него сильная аллергия на соль.
'He has a severe allergy to salt.' Lyova maintains a steady view at this moment, pairing "silnaya" ("strong") with "allergiya" ("an allergy") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Говорит, это не ресторан, а забегаловка.
'He says this is not a restaurant, but a dive.' Lyova sets a resolute attitude right away, building the phrase around "govorit" ("talks") and "restoran" ("restaurant") for a crisp, natural delivery.
Вы что там, совсем с ума сошли?
'Have you completely lost your minds in there?' Nagiyev wonders naturally as the talk turns, linking "tam" ("there"), "sovsem" ("at all"), and "uma" ("mind") in one brisk exchange.
Император уже полжизни заказ ждёт!

'The Emperor has been waiting half his life for his order!' Nagiyev keeps a warm manner as the scene unfolds, leaning on "imperator" ("himself") before closing the thought with "uzhe" ("already, now").
Я перед ним анекдоты рассказываю.
'I am telling jokes in front of him.' Nagiyev shares a wry tone on the spot, joining "anekdoty" ("front") to "rasskazyvayu" ("to tell, to talk about") so every word pulls its weight.
Кто сегодня готовил это блюдо?
'Who cooked this dish today?' Nagiyev wonders earnestly across the room, pairing "segodnya" ("today") with "gotovil" ("prepared, made") to get the point across in plain spoken Russian.
Слушай, через минуту блюдо будет готово.
'Listen, in a minute the dish will be ready.' Barinov brings a playful direction in the conversation, putting "slushay" ("listen") alongside "minutu" ("a minute") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Император недоволен, он нас уничтожит!
'The Emperor is displeased, he will destroy us!' Nagiyev adopts a steady direction right away, combining "imperator" ("himself") and "nedovolen" ("dissatisfied") so the key meaning lands right away.
Кстати, а где мой клон?
'By the way, where is my clone?' Barinov presses firmly from the start, linking "kstati" ("by the way") directly with "gde" ("where"), since Russian drops "is" and "are" in the present.
Он должен был меня заменить.
'He was supposed to replace me.' Barinov adopts a brisk footing as they talk, building the phrase around "dolzhen" ("has to, must") and "byl" ("was") for a crisp, natural delivery.
А он вас уже заменил, шеф!

'He has already replaced you, chef!' Lyova displays an honest line beside Barinov, building the phrase around "uzhe" ("already, now") and "zamenil" ("to replace") for a crisp, natural delivery. Now let's hear the whole scene again at natural speed.

Он должен был меня заменить.

That wraps up this scene as when the galactic Emperor rejects his dish because of a salt allergy and threatens to vaporize the restaurant, Barinov discovers his clone ruined the meal before waking up. See you next time!
